bill.title: Shenandoah Mountain Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 214.
subjects: Wilderness and natural areas, wildlife refuges, wild rivers, habitats
bill.officialSummary: Shenandoah Mountain Act This bill establishes the Shenandoah Mountain National Scenic Area, consisting of approximately 92,562 acres of National Forest System land in Virginia in the George Washington and Jefferson National Forest. The bill designates specified lands in the forest as wilderness and as components of the National Wilderness Preservation System, including (1) 5,088 acres as the Skidmore Fork Wilderness, (2) 3,568 acres as the Lynn Hollow Wilderness, (3) 12,461 acres as the Little River Wilderness, and (4) 5,779 acres as the Beech Lick Knob Wilderness.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would create a new national scenic area covering approximately 92,562 acres of federal forest land in Virginia within the George Washington and Jefferson National Forest. It would also designate four separate wilderness areas totaling about 26,896 acres within that forest, adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System. These designations would impose stricter land-use and conservation rules on the affected acreage.

industries.rationale: Wilderness and scenic-area designations typically restrict or prohibit mineral extraction and energy development on the designated lands.
Wilderness designations generally prohibit new mining claims and mineral extraction activities on the affected acreage.
Creation of a national scenic area and wilderness areas may affect tourism, recreation services, and visitor access in the region.
Wilderness designations can affect grazing permits and other agricultural uses of federal forest land, though the bill does not specify existing uses.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would set up the Shenandoah Mountain National Scenic Area, consisting of approximately 92,562 acres of National Forest System land in Virginia in the George Washington and Jefferson National Forest.
plain.whoItTouches: People who visit public land, and people who live beside it. People who live near or work on federal land.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
